questions.question_text: A parabola $y = f(x) = (x - 3)^2 - 4$ has its vertex at $(3, -4)$ and opens upwards. Which statement correctly describes the graph of its derivative $y = f'(x)$?

options.text: A straight line with positive gradient crossing the $x$-axis at $(3, 0)$.
A parabola with vertex at $(3, 0)$ opening upwards.
options.why: Confused the derivative of a quadratic with another quadratic curve.

options.text: A straight line with negative gradient crossing the $x$-axis at $(3, 0)$.
options.why: Reversed the slope of the linear derivative function.
Confused the derivative function with the horizontal tangent line at the vertex.

questions.solution_text:
$f(x) = (x - 3)^2 - 4 = x^2 - 6x + 5$
$f'(x) = 2x - 6 = 2(x - 3)$
The derivative is a straight line with gradient $2 > 0$ and $x$-intercept $(3, 0)$.

questions.question_text: A cubic curve $y = f(x)$ has a local maximum at $(-2, 5)$ and a local minimum at $(2, -3)$. What are the $x$-intercepts of $y = f'(x)$ and where does $y = f'(x)$ lie below the $x$-axis?

options.text: $x$-intercepts at $x = -2$ and $x = 2$; below the $x$-axis for $-2 < x < 2$.
$x$-intercepts at $x = -3$ and $x = 5$; below the $x$-axis for $-3 < x < 5$.
options.why: Used the y-coordinates of the turning points as intercepts instead of the x-coordinates.

options.text: $x$-intercepts at $x = -2$ and $x = 2$; below the $x$-axis for $x < -2$ and $x > 2$.
options.why: Reversed the region where the derivative is negative.
Assumed a cubic derivative has only a single intercept at the inflection point.

questions.solution_text:
The stationary points of $f(x)$ at $x = -2$ and $x = 2$ give $x$-intercepts of $f'(x)$ at $x = -2$ and $x = 2$.
$f(x)$ decreases between its turning points (for $-2 < x < 2$), so $f'(x) < 0$ (below the $x$-axis) for $-2 < x < 2$.

questions.question_text: A curve $y = f(x)$ has stationary points at $x = -4$, $x = 0$, and $x = 3$. At which values of $x$ does the graph of $y = f'(x)$ intersect the $x$-axis?

options.why: Omitted the stationary point at the origin x = 0.
Swapped the signs of the negative and positive stationary points.
Assumed only the inflection point produces an intercept on the derivative.

questions.solution_text:
Stationary points on $y = f(x)$ occur where $f'(x) = 0$.
Therefore, the $x$-intercepts of $y = f'(x)$ are precisely $x = -4, 0, 3$.

questions.question_text: The graph of $y = f'(x)$ is a parabola opening upwards with $x$-intercepts at $x = -1$ and $x = 5$. At which $x$-value does $y = f(x)$ have a local maximum?

options.why: Identified the local minimum where f' changes from negative to positive instead of local max.
Selected the vertex of the derivative graph instead of a stationary point.
Chose the y-intercept of the derivative graph rather than the point where gradient changes sign.

questions.solution_text:
Since $y = f'(x)$ is an upward parabola with roots $-1$ and $5$:
For $x < -1$, $f'(x) > 0$; for $-1 < x < 5$, $f'(x) < 0$; for $x > 5$, $f'(x) > 0$.
At $x = -1$, $f'(x)$ changes from positive to negative, which corresponds to a local maximum on $y = f(x)$.

questions.question_text: The function $y = f(x)$ is strictly increasing for all $x$ and has horizontal asymptotes $y = 0$ as $x \to -\infty$ and $y = 4$ as $x \to +\infty$. Which statement correctly describes the graph of $y = f'(x)$?

options.why: Confused an increasing function with a decreasing function.
Confused the derivative limit with the function horizontal asymptote value.
Confused having asymptotes with being a constant horizontal line.

questions.solution_text:
Since $f(x)$ is strictly increasing, $f'(x) > 0$ for all $x$.
As $x \to \pm\infty$, the curve flattens towards horizontal asymptotes, so its gradient approaches zero: $f'(x) \to 0$.

questions.question_text: A quartic function $y = f(x)$ has three stationary points: local minima at $x = -3$ and $x = 3$, and a local maximum at $x = 0$. What is the shape of $y = f'(x)$ and where does it cross the $x$-axis?

options.text: A cubic curve crossing the $x$-axis at $x = -3$, $x = 0$, and $x = 3$.
A parabola with vertex at $(0, 0)$ crossing the $x$-axis at $x = -3$ and $x = 3$.
options.why: Differentiated a degree 4 polynomial to degree 2 instead of degree 3.

options.text: A quartic curve with turning points at $x = -3, 0, 3$.
options.why: Assumed the derivative has the same degree and turning points as the original function.

options.text: A cubic curve crossing the $x$-axis at $x = -3$ and $x = 3$ only.
options.why: Omitted the stationary point at x = 0 as an x-intercept of the derivative.

questions.solution_text:
Differentiating a degree 4 polynomial produces a degree 3 cubic polynomial.
The three stationary points $x = -3, 0, 3$ become the three $x$-intercepts of $y = f'(x)$.

questions.question_text: The graph of $y = f'(x)$ touches the $x$-axis at $x = 2$ but remains non-negative ($f'(x) \geq 0$) for all real $x$. What feature does the original graph $y = f(x)$ have at $x = 2$?

options.why: Assumed touching the x-axis from above produces a turning point minimum on f(x).
Assumed a stationary point must be a turning point.
Confused a zero derivative with a point of discontinuity.

questions.solution_text:
At $x = 2$, $f'(2) = 0$, so $x = 2$ is a stationary point.
Because $f'(x) > 0$ for both $x < 2$ and $x > 2$, the derivative does not change sign.
Therefore, $y = f(x)$ has a horizontal point of inflection at $x = 2$.

questions.question_text: The graph of $y = f(x)$ has a horizontal point of inflection at $(1, 2)$ and is strictly increasing for all $x \neq 1$. What is the shape of the graph of $y = f'(x)$?

options.text: A parabola opening upwards with vertex at $(1, 0)$ touching the $x$-axis.
A straight line passing through $(1, 0)$ with positive slope.
options.why: Reduced the degree of the cubic by two instead of one.

options.text: A parabola opening downwards with vertex at $(1, 0)$.
options.why: Chose a negative derivative for a function that is strictly increasing.

options.text: A parabola crossing the $x$-axis at two distinct points symmetric about $x = 1$.
options.why: Gave two turning points instead of a single horizontal point of inflection.

questions.solution_text:
A cubic with horizontal inflection at $x = 1$ has derivative $f'(x) = k(x - 1)^2$ with $k > 0$.
This is an upward parabola touching the $x$-axis at its vertex $(1, 0)$ without crossing it.
